title: Ionizing radiation
summary: Ionizing radiation carries enough energy to knock electrons off atoms. It comes from natural sources like cosmic rays and radon and from artificial ones like X-ray tubes and reactors. It is very useful, but it harms health without control, so exposure is limited using time, distance, shielding, containment, dose limits, and monitoring.

key_points.point: Ionizing radiation has enough energy per photon or particle to detach electrons from atoms or molecules.
key_points.explanation: This ability to ionize defines the radiation. Gamma rays, X-rays, and higher-energy ultraviolet are ionizing. Lower-energy ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves, and nearly all laser light are not. The boundary is not sharp and depends on the definition used.

key_points.point: Exposure to ionizing radiation is a health hazard unless protective measures are taken, with deterministic and stochastic effects.
key_points.explanation: High acute doses cause deterministic effects such as radiation burns and radiation sickness, from cells dying or malfunctioning. Stochastic effects, meaning cancer and heritable effects, come from mutation of body or reproductive cells. Cancer often appears years or decades after exposure.

key_points.point: Alpha, beta, gamma, and neutron radiation penetrate matter very differently, so each needs different shielding.
key_points.explanation: Alpha particles are stopped by a few centimeters of air or the top layer of skin. Beta particles are stopped by sheet metal such as aluminium, ideally low-atomic-number material to limit bremsstrahlung X-rays. Gamma rays and neutrons need lead, concrete, or water. Hydrogen-rich materials are the best neutron shields because fast neutrons knock protons out of hydrogen. Half-value thickness describes how much material cuts radiation by half.

key_points.point: Exposure is limited by time, distance, shielding, and containment.
key_points.explanation: Spend less time near a source, stay farther away (intensity falls sharply with distance, following an inverse-square law), and put suitable material in between. Containment combines shielding with isolation, keeping materials in the smallest possible space, such as a hot cell or glove box, often at slightly reduced air pressure. Reactors operate within closed systems with multiple barriers.

key_points.point: Occupational and public exposures have recommended limits and are monitored.
key_points.explanation: The ICRP recommends an occupational limit of 50 mSv in a single year, with a maximum of 100 mSv over five consecutive years. For the public it recommends an average of 1 mSv of effective dose per year, excluding medical and occupational exposures. Workers are monitored with dosimeters, and a legal record of dose is kept under national regulations and local licence constraints.

key_points.point: The linear no-threshold (LNT) model is the most widely accepted way to estimate cancer risk.
key_points.explanation: LNT says cancer incidence rises linearly with effective dose, at 5.5% per sievert. If it is correct, natural background radiation is the most hazardous source for the general public, with medical imaging a close second. Models that predict risk levels remain controversial.

key_points.point: Radiation comes from natural and artificial sources, and background radiation averages about 3 mSv per year worldwide.
key_points.explanation: About 80% of background dose is natural, from cosmic rays, radioactive decay, and radon, a gas that builds up in poorly ventilated houses and is the largest cause of lung cancer among non-smokers. Medical procedures make up most of the human-made 20%. Airline crews receive more average dose than any other worker group, and astronauts beyond Earth's magnetic field face solar and cosmic radiation.

key_points.point: Ionizing radiation cannot be sensed by humans, so instruments and warning signs are needed.
key_points.explanation: Instruments such as Geiger counters detect and measure it. The trefoil on a yellow background marks controlled areas or places where radiation is significantly above background, and the red ISO 21482 symbol warns people not to dismantle devices housing dangerous sources.

terms.definition: The process of detaching electrons from atoms or molecules.
A helium-4 nucleus of two protons and two neutrons, strongly ionizing but weakly penetrating.
A high-energy, high-speed electron or positron emitted in beta decay.
A photon produced within the nucleus by nuclear reactions or decay, absorbed gradually in dense material.
"Braking radiation": X-rays produced when high-energy beta particles interact with matter.
A model in which cancer incidence rises linearly with effective dose, at 5.5% per sievert.
Ionizing radiation people are always exposed to from natural and human-made sources.
The thickness of a material that reduces radiation by half, depending on the material and the type and energy of the radiation.
A combination of shielding and isolation that confines radioactive materials in the smallest possible space and keeps them out of the environment.
An instrument used to monitor the radiation exposure of workers.

common_misconceptions: All ultraviolet light and all lasers are ionizing; in fact only the higher-energy ultraviolet part is ionizing, and nearly all laser light is not.
Neutral radiation is harmless because it is not charged; in fact photons and neutrons cause substantial ionization indirectly through secondary particles.
Nuclear power is the main source of human-made radiation exposure to the public; the source says medical procedures are by far the most significant.
